Discrete time series and contexts of models

Source: vignettes/dts-and-contexts.Rmd
dts-and-contexts.Rmd
library(mixvlmc)

This vignette covers two complementary aspects of mixvlmc: the representation of the discrete time series used to estimate models, and the detailed exploration of the contexts of fitted models. It assumes some familiarity with the notions introduced in vignette("context-trees") (contexts, context trees, contexts() with frequency, and the basic node functions find_sequence(), is_context(), children(), counts() and positions()), in vignette("variable-length-markov-chains") and in vignette("covlmc").

Discrete time series

Creating a discrete time series

Since version 0.3.0, mixvlmc represents discrete time series by objects of class dts, created by the dts() function. A dts stores the time series together with its state space, i.e. the set of values that the series can take. A dts can be built from a numeric, character, factor or logical vector. When the state space is not specified, it is computed from the vector in a way that depends on its type. For numeric and character vectors, the state space consists of the unique values of the series, in increasing order:

x_num <- dts(c(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3))
x_num
#> Discrete time series of length 6 with state space 1, 2, 3
#>  3 1 2 2 1 ...
states(x_num)
#> [1] 1 2 3
x_chr <- dts(c("b", "a", "c", "a", "b"))
states(x_chr)
#> [1] "a" "b" "c"

For a factor, the state space is given by the levels of the factor, including levels that do not appear in the series, and in the order of the levels:

x_fct <- dts(factor(c("low", "high", "low"),
  levels = c("low", "medium", "high")
))
x_fct
#> Discrete time series of length 3 with state space low, medium, high
#>  low high low

For a logical vector, the state space is always c(FALSE, TRUE):

x_lgl <- dts(c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE))
states(x_lgl)
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE

By default, only the first 5 values of the series are printed, but this can be changed with the n parameter of print():

set.seed(0)
x_long <- dts(sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 50, replace = TRUE))
x_long
#> Discrete time series of length 50 with state space A, B, C
#>  B A C A B ...
print(x_long, n = 15)
#> Discrete time series of length 50 with state space A, B, C
#>  B A C A B A C C B B C C A A A ...

is_dts() tests whether an object is a discrete time series, states() returns its state space and dts_data() recovers the original series as a vector (of the same type as the state space):

is_dts(x_chr)
#> [1] TRUE
is_dts(c("b", "a", "c"))
#> [1] FALSE
dts_data(x_chr)
#> [1] "b" "a" "c" "a" "b"
dts_data(x_fct)
#> [1] low  high low 
#> Levels: low medium high

The length of a dts is given by length() and a dts can be subsetted with [. The result is a dts with the same state space, even if some states do not appear in the subset:

length(x_long)
#> [1] 50
x_long[1:2]
#> Discrete time series of length 2 with state space A, B, C
#>  B A

Discrete time series cannot contain missing values:

try(dts(c("a", NA, "b")))
#> Error in validate_dts(x, vals) : 
#>   discrete time series cannot contain missing values

Specifying the state space

The state space can be given explicitly with the vals parameter of dts(). This has two uses. First, it sets the order of the states, which is the order used by all the functions of the package (for instance to order the columns of the results of contexts() or predict(), or the probabilities displayed by draw()). Second, the state space can include states that do not appear in the series:

x_abc <- dts(c("b", "a", "b"), vals = c("c", "b", "a"))
x_abc
#> Discrete time series of length 3 with state space c, b, a
#>  b a b

When vals is given, dts() checks that the series only contains values of the state space:

try(dts(c("a", "d"), vals = c("a", "b", "c")))
#> Error : x contains unknown states

Why use a discrete time series object?

All the estimation functions of the package (ctx_tree(), vlmc(), covlmc(), tune_vlmc() and tune_covlmc()) accept either a plain vector or a dts. In the former case, the vector is converted with dts() using the default state space. Using a dts directly is useful mainly when the state space of the model cannot be deduced reliably from the series used to estimate it, a common situation when several series are analysed with the same state space.

Let us consider the household electricity consumption data set powerconsumption. As in vignette("covlmc"), the active power is discretised into three levels. The following function extracts the discretised series of some weeks of the data set (as a character vector):

power_levels <- c("low", "typical", "high")
power_weeks <- function(weeks) {
  pc <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week %in% weeks, ]
  as.character(cut(pc$active_power,
    breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
    labels = power_levels
  ))
}
week_33 <- power_weeks(33)
week_35 <- power_weeks(35)
table(week_33)
#> week_33
#>     low typical 
#>     925      83
table(week_35)
#> week_35
#>    high     low typical 
#>      28     891      89

The consumption is very low during week 33, in August (probably because of holidays), and the high level is never observed. A model estimated on this week from the character vector has therefore only two states and it cannot be used on week 35:

model_33_raw <- vlmc(week_33)
states(model_33_raw)
#> [1] "low"     "typical"
try(loglikelihood(model_33_raw, newdata = week_35))
#> Error : x contains unknown states

If we specify the state space with a dts, the model knows that the high level exists:

week_33_dts <- dts(week_33, vals = power_levels)
model_33 <- vlmc(week_33_dts)
model_33
#> VLMC context tree on low, typical, high [C++]
#>  cutoff: 2.996 (quantile: 0.05)
#>  Number of contexts: 42 
#>  Maximum context length: 24
loglikelihood(model_33, newdata = week_35)
#> 'log Lik.' -Inf (df= 84, nb obs.= 984, initial="truncated")

The log likelihood is now computed, and its value, \(-\infty\), tells us that week 35 is impossible according to the model of week 33, as the high level was never observed during that week. The predicted probabilities include all the states of the state space, in the specified order (the last row is the prediction of the state that follows the series, see predict.vlmc()):

predict(model_33, newdata = week_35[1:5], type = "probs")
#>            low    typical high
#> [1,] 0.9176587 0.08234127    0
#> [2,] 0.9155844 0.08441558    0
#> [3,] 0.9088757 0.09112426    0
#> [4,] 0.9009126 0.09908735    0
#> [5,] 0.8942029 0.10579710    0
#> [6,] 0.8847403 0.11525974    0

Notice that the new data (newdata in loglikelihood() and predict(), init in simulate() or the sequence given to find_sequence()) can be given as a plain vector or as a dts. In both cases, it is interpreted in the state space of the model: a dts with a different state space is accepted provided its values belong to the state space of the model. For instance, the following call computes the log likelihood of week 34, in which the high level is also absent, with the model of week 33:

week_34_dts <- dts(power_weeks(34))
states(week_34_dts)
#> [1] "low"     "typical"
loglikelihood(model_33, newdata = week_34_dts)
#> 'log Lik.' -201.5814 (df= 84, nb obs.= 984, initial="truncated")

When the series is a factor, its levels define the state space, so discretising directly with cut() (without the conversion to character used above) also gives a model with three states:

states(vlmc(factor(week_33, levels = power_levels)))
#> [1] low     typical high   
#> Levels: low typical high

Finally, simulate() does not return a dts but a vector of the same type as the state space of the model (here a character vector), whose values are taken from this state space. It can be converted into a dts with the same state space as follows:

sim_33 <- simulate(model_33, 20, seed = 0)
sim_33
#>  [1] "low"     "low"     "low"     "low"     "typical" "low"     "low"    
#>  [8] "low"     "low"     "low"     "low"     "low"     "low"     "low"    
#> [15] "low"     "low"     "low"     "low"     "typical" "low"
dts(sim_33, vals = states(model_33))
#> Discrete time series of length 20 with state space low, typical, high
#>  low low low low typical ...

Contexts of a VLMC

In the rest of this vignette, we use a VLMC estimated on week 5 of the electricity consumption data set. We keep the positions of the contexts in the time series with keep_match = TRUE (they are not kept by default). The model is estimated with the default C++ backend (see vlmc()), but all the functions described below work in the same way with the R backend (backend = "R").

week_5 <- dts(power_weeks(5), vals = power_levels)
model_5 <- vlmc(week_5, keep_match = TRUE)
model_5
#> VLMC context tree on low, typical, high [C++]
#>  cutoff: 2.996 (quantile: 0.05)
#>  Number of contexts: 26 
#>  Maximum context length: 9
draw(model_5)
#> ▪ (0.1667, 0.5496, 0.2837)
#> ├─ low (0.7665, 0.2335, 0)
#> │  └─ low (0.7638, 0.2362, 0)
#> │     └─ low (0.7917, 0.2083, 0)
#> │        └─ low (0.8133, 0.1867, 0)
#> │           ├─ low (0.9167, 0.08333, 0)
#> │           │  └─ low (0.9091, 0.09091, 0)
#> │           │     └─ low (0.9, 0.1, 0)
#> │           │        └─ low (0.8889, 0.1111, 0)
#> │           │           └─ typical (0.4, 0.6, 0)
#> │           └─ typical (0.4, 0.6, 0)
#> ├─ typical (0.0704, 0.8466, 0.08303)
#> │  ├─ low (0.3846, 0.5385, 0.07692)
#> │  ├─ typical (0.04691, 0.8849, 0.06823)
#> │  │  └─ typical (0.04337, 0.8892, 0.06747)
#> │  │     └─ low (0.2941, 0.6471, 0.05882)
#> │  └─ high (0.04444, 0.7111, 0.2444)
#> └─ high (0.003497, 0.1573, 0.8392)
#>    ├─ typical (0.02174, 0.2826, 0.6957)
#>    │  └─ typical (0.03125, 0.3125, 0.6562)
#>    │     └─ high (0.3333, 0.6667, 0)
#>    └─ high (0, 0.1333, 0.8667)
#>       └─ high (0, 0.1106, 0.8894)
#>          └─ high (0, 0.0973, 0.9027)
#>             └─ high (0, 0.1018, 0.8982)
#>                └─ high (0, 0.1, 0.9)
#>                   └─ high (0, 0.1037, 0.8963)
#>                      └─ typical (0, 0.3571, 0.6429)

Two representations

contexts() gives two representations of the contexts of a model. By default, it returns a list of ctx_node objects, one per context, which can be explored with the node functions described in the next section:

ctxs_5 <- contexts(model_5)
ctxs_5
#> Contexts:
#>  typical, high, high, high, high, high, high, high
#>  high, high, high, high, high, high, high
#>  high, high, high, high, high, high
#>  high, high, high, high, high
#>  high, high, high, high
#>  high, high, high
#>  high, high
#>  high, typical, typical, high
#>  typical, typical, high
#>  typical, high
#>  high
#>  low, typical
#>  low, typical, typical, typical
#>  typical, typical, typical
#>  typical, typical
#>  high, typical
#>  typical, low, low, low, low
#>  typical, low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low
#>  low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low
#>  low, low, low, low, low, low, low
#>  low, low, low, low, low, low
#>  low, low, low, low, low
#>  low, low, low, low
#>  low, low, low
#>  low, low
#>  low

With sequence = TRUE, or as soon as additional information is requested (see below), the function returns a data frame with one row per context. Its first column, context, is a list: each element is a vector of states (of the same type as states(model_5)) that represents a context. As the default printing of such a column is truncated, we define a small helper function that replaces each context by a character string, only for display purposes:

flat_contexts <- function(ctx_df) {
  ctx_df$context <- vapply(ctx_df$context, paste, character(1), collapse = ", ")
  ctx_df
}
ctx_df_5 <- contexts(model_5, sequence = TRUE)
ctx_df_5$context[[1]]
#> [1] "typical" "high"    "high"    "high"    "high"    "high"    "high"   
#> [8] "high"

Contexts are written by default in temporal order (the most recent state is on the right), while reverse = TRUE uses the reverse order of Bühlmann and Wyner (the most recent state is on the left), which corresponds to the paths from the root in the representation of draw():

head(flat_contexts(contexts(model_5, sequence = TRUE, reverse = TRUE)))
#>                                             context
#> 1 high, high, high, high, high, high, high, typical
#> 2          high, high, high, high, high, high, high
#> 3                high, high, high, high, high, high
#> 4                      high, high, high, high, high
#> 5                            high, high, high, high
#> 6                                  high, high, high

The parameter reverse has the same effect on the list representation and can also be given to the print() function of a list of contexts (print(ctxs_5, reverse = TRUE)).

The additional columns depend on the parameters of contexts() and on the class of the model, as summarised below (contexts() accepts the same parameters for both backends of ctx_tree() and vlmc(), but the order of the contexts may differ from one backend to the other).

parameter ctx_tree vlmc covlmc columns
frequency yes yes yes freq, one per state if "detailed"
positions yes yes yes positions
local no yes yes (modifies the counts)
cutoff no yes no cutoff
metrics no yes yes accuracy, auc
model no no yes coef or model
hsize no no yes hsize
merging no no yes merged

Counts

As for context trees, frequency = "total" adds a freq column with the number of occurrences of each context in the time series (not including a possible final occurrence not followed by any state), while frequency = "detailed" adds in addition one column per state with the number of times the context is followed by this state:

flat_contexts(contexts(model_5, frequency = "detailed"))
#>                                              context freq low typical high
#> 1  typical, high, high, high, high, high, high, high   14   0       5    9
#> 2           high, high, high, high, high, high, high  135   0      14  121
#> 3                 high, high, high, high, high, high  150   0      15  135
#> 4                       high, high, high, high, high  167   0      17  150
#> 5                             high, high, high, high  185   0      18  167
#> 6                                   high, high, high  208   0      23  185
#> 7                                         high, high  240   0      32  208
#> 8                       high, typical, typical, high    3   1       2    0
#> 9                             typical, typical, high   32   1      10   21
#> 10                                     typical, high   46   1      13   32
#> 11                                              high  286   1      45  240
#> 12                                      low, typical   39  15      21    3
#> 13                    low, typical, typical, typical   17   5      11    1
#> 14                         typical, typical, typical  415  18     369   28
#> 15                                  typical, typical  469  22     415   32
#> 16                                     high, typical   45   2      32   11
#> 17                       typical, low, low, low, low   15   6       9    0
#> 18   typical, low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low    5   2       3    0
#> 19            low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low   45  40       5    0
#> 20                 low, low, low, low, low, low, low   50  45       5    0
#> 21                      low, low, low, low, low, low   55  50       5    0
#> 22                           low, low, low, low, low   60  55       5    0
#> 23                                low, low, low, low   75  61      14    0
#> 24                                     low, low, low   96  76      20    0
#> 25                                          low, low  127  97      30    0
#> 26                                               low  167 128      39    0

These counts are the ones used to estimate the transition probabilities of the model shown by draw(): for instance, the probabilities associated with the context low are obtained by dividing the counts of the low row by its freq value.

In a VLMC, a context can be the suffix of longer contexts. For instance, high, high is the last part of high, high, high. The counts above include all the occurrences of high, high, including the ones that are the last part of an occurrence of high, high, high. With local = TRUE, the counts include only the occurrences of the context that are not the last part of a longer context, that is the time steps at which the context is the one actually used by the model to predict the next state:

ctx_local_5 <- contexts(model_5, frequency = "detailed", local = TRUE)
flat_contexts(ctx_local_5)
#>                                              context freq low typical high
#> 1  typical, high, high, high, high, high, high, high   14   0       5    9
#> 2           high, high, high, high, high, high, high  121   0       9  112
#> 3                 high, high, high, high, high, high   15   0       1   14
#> 4                       high, high, high, high, high   17   0       2   15
#> 5                             high, high, high, high   18   0       1   17
#> 6                                   high, high, high   23   0       5   18
#> 7                                         high, high   32   0       9   23
#> 8                       high, typical, typical, high    3   1       2    0
#> 9                             typical, typical, high   29   0       8   21
#> 10                                     typical, high   14   0       3   11
#> 11                                              high    0   0       0    0
#> 12                                      low, typical   39  15      21    3
#> 13                    low, typical, typical, typical   17   5      11    1
#> 14                         typical, typical, typical  398  13     358   27
#> 15                                  typical, typical   54   4      46    4
#> 16                                     high, typical   45   2      32   11
#> 17                       typical, low, low, low, low   15   6       9    0
#> 18   typical, low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low    5   2       3    0
#> 19            low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low   40  38       2    0
#> 20                 low, low, low, low, low, low, low    5   5       0    0
#> 21                      low, low, low, low, low, low    5   5       0    0
#> 22                           low, low, low, low, low    5   5       0    0
#> 23                                low, low, low, low    0   0       0    0
#> 24                                     low, low, low   21  15       6    0
#> 25                                          low, low   31  21      10    0
#> 26                                               low   40  31       9    0

Each time step is associated with at most one context, so that the sum of the local counts, 1006, is smaller than the length of the time series, 1008 (the first time steps do not have a long enough past and the last state is not followed by any state). Some contexts have zero local counts. For instance, the context high exists only because the model must define a next state distribution after the sequence low, high, which never appears in the time series: the context high is used only for this unobserved sequence, while all the actual occurrences of high are covered by longer contexts.

Cut off values

For a VLMC, cutoff adds a cutoff column that summarises, for each context, the likelihood ratio test that compares the next state distribution of the context with the one of its parent, the context obtained by removing its oldest state. With cutoff = "native" the value is the log likelihood ratio, while cutoff = "quantile" gives it in the quantile scale (the p-value of the test). See cutoff(), prune(), vignette("variable-length-markov-chains") and vignette("model-selection") for details on these two scales.

flat_contexts(contexts(model_5, cutoff = "quantile"))
#>                                              context       cutoff
#> 1  typical, high, high, high, high, high, high, high 4.109563e-02
#> 2           high, high, high, high, high, high, high 9.898744e-01
#> 3                 high, high, high, high, high, high 9.973425e-01
#> 4                       high, high, high, high, high 9.811938e-01
#> 5                             high, high, high, high 8.419314e-01
#> 6                                   high, high, high 6.121980e-01
#> 7                                         high, high 2.441270e-01
#> 8                       high, typical, typical, high 2.059937e-02
#> 9                             typical, typical, high 8.660173e-01
#> 10                                     typical, high 3.209832e-02
#> 11                                              high 1.249709e-87
#> 12                                      low, typical 1.459397e-07
#> 13                    low, typical, typical, typical 2.639095e-03
#> 14                         typical, typical, typical 9.391320e-01
#> 15                                  typical, typical 4.308507e-02
#> 16                                     high, typical 4.617865e-03
#> 17                       typical, low, low, low, low 1.929706e-03
#> 18   typical, low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low 3.136127e-02
#> 19            low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low 9.705409e-01
#> 20                 low, low, low, low, low, low, low 9.760067e-01
#> 21                      low, low, low, low, low, low 9.800842e-01
#> 22                           low, low, low, low, low 7.841197e-02
#> 23                                low, low, low, low 8.961669e-01
#> 24                                     low, low, low 8.082117e-01
#> 25                                          low, low 9.974477e-01
#> 26                                               low 4.762280e-71

The model was estimated with the default alpha = 0.05 and a context with a quantile value lower than alpha is significantly different from its parent. Some contexts have larger values: they are kept in the model because one of their descendants in the context tree is significant (for instance a context low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low is kept because its extension typical, low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low is significant). Notice that those values are not those reported by cutoff(model_5) (see the dedicated section in the documentation of contexts.vlmc()).

Predictive metrics

With metrics = TRUE, contexts() adds predictive quality metrics for each context, computed on the time steps at which the context is used by the model (i.e. the ones counted by local = TRUE):

flat_contexts(contexts(model_5,
  frequency = "total", local = TRUE,
  metrics = TRUE
))
#>                                              context freq  accuracy auc
#> 1  typical, high, high, high, high, high, high, high   14 0.6428571  NA
#> 2           high, high, high, high, high, high, high  121 0.9256198  NA
#> 3                 high, high, high, high, high, high   15 0.9333333  NA
#> 4                       high, high, high, high, high   17 0.8823529  NA
#> 5                             high, high, high, high   18 0.9444444  NA
#> 6                                   high, high, high   23 0.7826087  NA
#> 7                                         high, high   32 0.7187500  NA
#> 8                       high, typical, typical, high    3 0.6666667  NA
#> 9                             typical, typical, high   29 0.7241379  NA
#> 10                                     typical, high   14 0.7857143  NA
#> 11                                              high    0       NaN  NA
#> 12                                      low, typical   39 0.5384615  NA
#> 13                    low, typical, typical, typical   17 0.6470588  NA
#> 14                         typical, typical, typical  398 0.8994975  NA
#> 15                                  typical, typical   54 0.8518519  NA
#> 16                                     high, typical   45 0.7111111  NA
#> 17                       typical, low, low, low, low   15 0.6000000  NA
#> 18   typical, low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low    5 0.6000000  NA
#> 19            low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low   40 0.9500000  NA
#> 20                 low, low, low, low, low, low, low    5 1.0000000  NA
#> 21                      low, low, low, low, low, low    5 1.0000000  NA
#> 22                           low, low, low, low, low    5 1.0000000  NA
#> 23                                low, low, low, low    0       NaN  NA
#> 24                                     low, low, low   21 0.7142857  NA
#> 25                                          low, low   31 0.6774194  NA
#> 26                                               low   40 0.7750000  NA

The accuracy column gives the proportion of those time steps at which the most probable state according to the context is the observed next state (it is not defined when the local count is zero). For a VLMC, the predicted probabilities are identical for all the time steps of a context, so that they cannot separate the next states: the auc column is therefore always missing. It is informative for a VLMC with covariates, see below. The metrics of the whole model are given by metrics(model_5) (see vignette("prediction")).

Positions

With positions = TRUE, a positions column gives for each context the list of its positions in the time series. A position of a context is the index \(t\) of its last state, so that \(x_{t+1}\) is the state that follows the context. Positions are available only if they have been kept during the estimation (keep_match = TRUE for vlmc(), keep_position = TRUE, the default, for ctx_tree(), always for covlmc()). As the positions are numerous, the column is better explored programmatically:

ctx_pos_5 <- contexts(model_5, frequency = "total", positions = TRUE)
head(ctx_pos_5$positions[[1]])
#> [1]  51 140 222 274 308 335

Positions cover all the occurrences of a context, not only the local ones. Unlike the counts, they include a possible final occurrence of the context, at the end of the time series, which is not followed by any state. Here the series ends with a sequence of low states, so the last time step, 1008, is a position of several contexts, which have therefore one more position than their count:

at_end <- sapply(ctx_pos_5$positions, function(pos) length(week_5) %in% pos)
ctx_pos_end <- flat_contexts(ctx_pos_5[at_end, c("context", "freq")])
ctx_pos_end$nb_positions <- lengths(ctx_pos_5$positions[at_end])
ctx_pos_end
#>                    context freq nb_positions
#> 22 low, low, low, low, low   60           61
#> 23      low, low, low, low   75           76
#> 24           low, low, low   96           97
#> 25                low, low  127          128
#> 26                     low  167          168

Contexts of a VLMC with covariates

We use now the data of vignette("covlmc"): weeks 15 and 16 of the electricity consumption data set, with a covariate that indicates whether the observation is made during the day or during the night.

elec_dts <- dts(power_weeks(c(15, 16)), vals = power_levels)
pc_15_16 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week %in% c(15, 16), ]
elec_cov <- data.frame(day = (pc_15_16$hour >= 7 & pc_15_16$hour <= 18))
elec_model <- covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov)
elec_model
#> VLMC with covariates context tree on low, typical, high 
#>  cutoff in quantile scale: 0.05
#>  Number of contexts: 7 
#>  Maximum context length: 3
draw(elec_model)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low ([ -1.681 • 0.4984 
#> │         -4.277 • -0.8766 ])
#> ├─ typical
#> │  ├─ low (0.3667, 0.5833, 0.05)
#> │  ├─ typical
#> │  │  ├─ low (0.4058, 0.5507, 0.04348)
#> │  │  ├─ typical ([ 1.792   • -14.02 ⁞ -3.253 ⁞ 18.34
#> │  │  │             -0.2877 • 16.01  ⁞ -36.08 ⁞ 20.01 ])
#> │  │  └─ high (0.05172, 0.8276, 0.1207)
#> │  └─ high (0.02817, 0.8169, 0.1549)
#> └─ high (0, 0.1864, 0.8136)

contexts() supports for COVLMC the frequency, local, positions and metrics parameters with the same meaning as for a VLMC. As the transition probabilities of a COVLMC depend on the covariates, the auc column is now informative: for a context whose model uses the covariates, it measures how well the probabilities computed by its model separate the possible next states. For a context whose model does not use the covariates, the predictions are constant and the AUC is 0.5 (or missing when some states never follow the context). The parameter hsize adds a column that gives the number of past values of the covariates used by the model of each context (0 for a context whose model does not use the covariates).

flat_contexts(contexts(elec_model,
  frequency = "detailed", hsize = TRUE,
  metrics = TRUE
))
#>                     context freq low typical high hsize  accuracy       auc
#> 1                       low  659 533     120    6     1 0.8088012 0.5653481
#> 2              low, typical  120  44      70    6     0 0.5833333 0.5000000
#> 3     low, typical, typical   69  28      38    3     0 0.5507246 0.5000000
#> 4 typical, typical, typical  655  49     568   38     3 0.8702290 0.6125158
#> 5    high, typical, typical   58   3      48    7     0 0.8275862 0.5000000
#> 6             high, typical   71   2      58   11     0 0.8169014 0.5000000
#> 7                      high  381   0      71  310     0 0.8136483        NA

The models themselves can be included in the data frame, either as their coefficients (model = "coef") or as the R objects produced by the estimation engine (model = "full", see covlmc() and the article Computing engines and control of VLMC with covariates for details about the engines). As for contexts, the corresponding column is a list:

ctx_coef <- contexts(elec_model, model = "coef")
ctx_coef$coef[[1]]
#>           [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -1.681411  0.4984117
#> [2,] -4.276666 -0.8766255

Finally, when the state space has at least three states, some contexts of a COVLMC can be merged: they share a single model. This happens for instance with a stricter cut off:

elec_model_merged <- covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, alpha = 1e-7)
draw(elec_model_merged)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low (0.8088, 0.1821, 0.009105)
#> ├─ typical
#> │  ├─ typical
#> │  │  ├─ low (0.4058, 0.5507, 0.04348)
#> │  │  ├─ typical (0.07481, 0.8672, 0.05802)
#> │  │  └─ high (0.05172, 0.8276, 0.1207)
#> │  └─ low, high (0.2408, 0.6702, 0.08901)
#> └─ high (0, 0.1864, 0.8136)

In this representation (see the article Drawing context trees and models), the leaf low, high denotes the two merged contexts low, typical and high, typical. contexts() reports merged contexts individually; merging = TRUE adds a merged column that identifies them:

flat_contexts(contexts(elec_model_merged,
  frequency = "total", merging = TRUE,
  metrics = TRUE
))
#>                     context freq  accuracy auc merged
#> 1                       low  659 0.8088012 0.5  FALSE
#> 2     low, typical, typical   69 0.5507246 0.5  FALSE
#> 3 typical, typical, typical  655 0.8671756 0.5  FALSE
#> 4    high, typical, typical   58 0.8275862 0.5  FALSE
#> 5              low, typical  120 0.6701571 0.5   TRUE
#> 6             high, typical   71 0.6701571 0.5   TRUE
#> 7                      high  381 0.8136483  NA  FALSE

As merged contexts share their model, they share also their metrics, computed on all the time steps of the merged contexts.

Navigating the contexts of a fitted model

Nodes of a VLMC

The function find_sequence() described in vignette("context-trees") also applies to fitted models. It returns NULL when the sequence is not represented in the context tree of the model:

find_sequence(model_5, c("low", "high"))
#> NULL

and a ctx_node object otherwise. Such a node can be a context or not:

node_typical <- find_sequence(model_5, "typical")
node_typical
#> Sequence [T]: typical 
#>  followed by low (39), typical (469), high (46)
is_context(node_typical)
#> [1] FALSE
node_th <- find_sequence(model_5, c("typical", "high"))
node_th
#> Context [T]: typical, high 
#>  followed by low (1), typical (13), high (32)
is_context(node_th)
#> [1] TRUE

The sequence represented by a node is obtained with as_sequence(). Its order (temporal or reverse) is the one used to create the node (by find_sequence() or contexts()), as reported by is_reversed(), and can be switched with rev() or overridden with the reverse parameter of as_sequence():

as_sequence(node_th)
#> [1] "typical" "high"
is_reversed(node_th)
#> [1] FALSE
node_th_rev <- rev(node_th)
node_th_rev
#> Context [R]: high, typical 
#>  followed by low (1), typical (13), high (32)
as_sequence(node_th_rev)
#> [1] "high"    "typical"
as_sequence(node_th_rev, reverse = FALSE)
#> [1] "typical" "high"

The context tree can be traversed with parent(), which removes the oldest state of the sequence (it returns NULL for the root of the tree, the empty sequence), and children(), which returns a list with one element per state (NULL when the corresponding extension of the sequence is not in the tree):

parent(node_th)
#> Context [T]: high 
#>  followed by low (1), typical (45), high (240)
parent(parent(node_th))
#> Sequence [T]:  
#>  followed by low (168), typical (554), high (286)
children(node_th)
#> $low
#> NULL
#> 
#> $typical
#> Context [T]: typical, typical, high 
#>  followed by low (1), typical (10), high (21)
#> 
#> $high
#> NULL

The counts() function supports the local parameter, as contexts():

counts(node_th)
#>   total low typical high
#> 1    46   1      13   32
counts(node_th, local = TRUE)
#>   total low typical high
#> 1    14   0       3   11

The positions of the node in the time series are given by positions(). As the state that follows a context at position \(t\) is \(x_{t+1}\), the counts can be recovered from the positions and the original series (a final occurrence at the end of the series would give a missing value, ignored by table()):

pos_th <- positions(node_th)
head(pos_th)
#> [1]  45  76 113 120 124 134
table(factor(dts_data(week_5)[pos_th + 1], levels = power_levels))
#> 
#>     low typical    high 
#>       1      13      32

Finally, cutoff() and metrics() give, for a single context, the information reported by the corresponding parameters of contexts(). Notice that cutoff() uses by default the quantile scale and modifies slightly the value to ensure that the context is pruned when the value is used in prune() (use raw = TRUE to get the exact value, see cutoff.ctx_node()):

cutoff(node_th)
#> [1] 0.03209832
cutoff(node_th, scale = "native", raw = TRUE)
#> [1] 3.438952
metrics(node_th)
#> Context [T]: typical, high 
#>  followed by low (1), typical (13), high (32)
#>  Confusion matrix: 
#>           low typical high 
#>   low     0   0       0    
#>   typical 0   0       0    
#>   high    0   3       11   
#>  Accuracy: 0.7857 
#>  AUC: NA

metrics() can only be applied to contexts:

try(metrics(node_typical))
#> Error in metrics.ctx_node(node_typical) : 
#>   the node is not a context, no metrics can be computed

Nodes of a VLMC with covariates

For a COVLMC, find_sequence() and contexts() return ctx_node_covlmc objects. In addition to the functions described above, model() gives the model of a context, either as its coefficients (by default) or as the full model, while covariate_memory() gives the number of past values of the covariates used by this model (as the hsize column of contexts()):

node_low <- find_sequence(elec_model, "low")
node_low
#> Context [T]: low 
#>  followed by low (533), typical (120), high (6)
model(node_low)
#>           [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -1.681411  0.4984117
#> [2,] -4.276666 -0.8766255
model(node_low, type = "full")
#> 
#> Call:
#> VGAM::vglm(formula = target ~ ., family = VGAM::multinomial(refLevel = 1), 
#>     data = mm, model = FALSE, x.arg = FALSE, y.arg = FALSE, maxit = getOption("mixvlmc.maxit"))
#> 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept):1 (Intercept):2   day_1TRUE:1   day_1TRUE:2 
#>    -1.6814114    -4.2766661     0.4984117    -0.8766255 
#> 
#> Degrees of Freedom: 1318 Total; 1314 Residual
#> Residual deviance: 684.6391 
#> Log-likelihood: -342.3195 
#> 
#> This is a multinomial logit model with 3 levels
covariate_memory(node_low)
#> [1] 1
metrics(node_low)
#> Context [T]: low 
#>  followed by low (533), typical (120), high (6)
#>  Confusion matrix: 
#>           low typical high 
#>   low     533 120     6    
#>   typical 0   0       0    
#>   high    0   0       0    
#>  Accuracy: 0.8088 
#>  AUC: 0.5653

Both functions return NULL for a node that is not a context:

node_tt <- find_sequence(elec_model, c("typical", "typical"))
is_context(node_tt)
#> [1] FALSE
model(node_tt)
#> NULL
covariate_memory(node_tt)
#> NULL

children() returns also ctx_node_covlmc objects. cutoff() gives the p-values of the likelihood ratio tests associated with a node, in quantile scale only (see cutoff.ctx_node_covlmc()): for a context, the test used to reduce the memory of its model (when it can lead to pruning) and, for a node with children, the tests used to replace its children by the node or to merge some of them. The union of these values over all the nodes is given by cutoff() applied to the model:

children(node_tt)
#> $low
#> Context [T]: low, typical, typical 
#>  followed by low (28), typical (38), high (3)
#> 
#> $typical
#> Context [T]: typical, typical, typical 
#>  followed by low (49), typical (568), high (38)
#> 
#> $high
#> Context [T]: high, typical, typical 
#>  followed by low (3), typical (48), high (7)
cutoff(node_low)
#> [1] 0.03453508
cutoff(node_tt)
#> [1] 0.0002688263
cutoff(elec_model)
#> [1] 3.453508e-02 7.217747e-03 2.688263e-04 2.670549e-07

is_merged() tells whether a context is merged with other contexts and merged_with() returns them (as a list with one element per state, in the same way as children(): the merged contexts differ only in their oldest state):

ctxs_merged <- contexts(elec_model_merged)
sapply(ctxs_merged, is_merged)
#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
node_lt <- find_sequence(elec_model_merged, c("low", "typical"))
merged_with(node_lt)
#> $low
#> NULL
#> 
#> $typical
#> NULL
#> 
#> $high
#> Context [T]: high, typical 
#>  followed by low (2), typical (58), high (11)
identical(model(node_lt), model(merged_with(node_lt)$high))
#> [1] TRUE
merged_with(find_sequence(elec_model_merged, "low"))
#> NULL

Worked examples

Predictable contexts and when they occur

Using the node functions, we can easily compute summary information about the contexts of a VLMC. The following function gives, for a context, its length, the most probable next state with its probability and the number of time steps at which the context is used by the model:

context_summary <- function(node) {
  freqs <- counts(node)
  probs <- unlist(freqs[, -1]) / freqs$total
  data.frame(
    context = paste(as_sequence(node), collapse = ", "),
    length = length(as_sequence(node)),
    next_state = names(probs)[which.max(probs)],
    probability = max(probs),
    usage = counts(node, frequency = "total", local = TRUE)
  )
}
summary_5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(contexts(model_5), context_summary))

We look for the contexts whose next state is almost deterministic (with a probability of at least 0.9) and that are actually used, ordered by decreasing length:

predictable <- summary_5[summary_5$probability >= 0.9 & summary_5$usage > 0, ]
predictable[order(predictable$length, decreasing = TRUE), ]
#>                               context length next_state probability usage
#> 20  low, low, low, low, low, low, low      7        low   0.9000000     5
#> 3  high, high, high, high, high, high      6       high   0.9000000    15
#> 21       low, low, low, low, low, low      6        low   0.9090909     5
#> 22            low, low, low, low, low      5        low   0.9166667     5
#> 5              high, high, high, high      4       high   0.9027027    18

Long sequences of the low level are likely to be followed by another low observation. The positions of the corresponding contexts can be related to other information available in the data set, for instance the hour of the day. Let us consider the longest context made only of low states:

all_low <- function(node) all(as_sequence(node) == "low")
low_ctxs <- Filter(all_low, contexts(model_5))
low_lengths <- sapply(low_ctxs, function(node) length(as_sequence(node)))
longest_low <- low_ctxs[[which.max(low_lengths)]]
longest_low
#> Context [T]: low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low 
#>  followed by low (40), typical (5), high (0)
pc_5 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
table(hour = pc_5$hour[positions(longest_low)])
#> hour
#>  2  3  4  5  6  7  8 17 21 
#>  2  6  6 11 12  5  1  1  1

As expected, those long periods of low consumption happen mostly during the night and the early morning.

Contexts that use the covariates

In a COVLMC, the dependency of the transition probabilities on the covariates is context specific. The contexts that actually use the covariates are obtained as follows:

uses_covariate <- function(node) covariate_memory(node) > 0
uses_cov <- Filter(uses_covariate, contexts(elec_model))
uses_cov
#> [[1]]
#> Context [T]: low 
#>  followed by low (533), typical (120), high (6)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Context [T]: typical, typical, typical 
#>  followed by low (49), typical (568), high (38)

To understand the effect of the covariate, we can for instance compare the empirical distribution of the next state during the day and during the night, using the positions of each context (the value of the covariate at the position of a context is the most recent one available to its model):

next_state_by_day <- function(node) {
  pos <- positions(node)
  ## remove a possible final occurrence
  pos <- pos[pos < length(elec_dts)]
  prop.table(table(
    day = elec_cov$day[pos],
    next_state = factor(dts_data(elec_dts)[pos + 1], levels = power_levels)
  ), margin = 1)
}
next_state_by_day(uses_cov[[1]])
#>        next_state
#> day             low     typical        high
#>   FALSE 0.833333333 0.155092593 0.011574074
#>   TRUE  0.762114537 0.233480176 0.004405286

After a low observation, the next observation is more likely to stay low at night than during the day. The comparison with a context whose model does not use the covariate shows smaller differences:

next_state_by_day(find_sequence(elec_model, "high"))
#>        next_state
#> day           low   typical      high
#>   FALSE 0.0000000 0.1737089 0.8262911
#>   TRUE  0.0000000 0.2023810 0.7976190

Finally, the predictive metrics of the contexts that use the covariates show that their AUC is larger than 0.5, the value obtained by a context whose model does not use the covariates (see the auc column of contexts() for elec_model above):

sapply(uses_cov, function(node) unlist(metrics(node)[c("accuracy", "auc")]))
#>               [,1]      [,2]
#> accuracy 0.8088012 0.8702290
#> auc      0.5653481 0.6125158
